title: An island out through the wire format and back, corner by corner
The island's history lays onto land worked out as it goes
why: The load-bearing half of a join, and the one the client cannot be made to do without a network: replaying `tile_change` over a world that is generated square by square as something asks for it. Get it wrong and a tree felled an hour ago stands again.

title: Where somebody has been survives the trip, and costs nothing to bring back
why: The fog of war lived in `localStorage` and nowhere else, so a refresh put a body in the middle of a black 4096 island. It is the island's to keep now — and a join must not have to work out every square anybody ever walked over in order to take it back.

title: The island handed over is the island come back to
why: Founding uploads what was rolled; joining works the ground out from the seed and never downloads it. Two generators that disagreed would put every player on ground the rules do not believe in, and nothing else in this suite would notice.

title: The ground a seed makes is the ground it made before
why: The land travelled once, at founding, and Postgres has held that copy ever since while every browser works the same ground out from the seed. So the generator is a wire format with one message in it, sent on founding day: change it and the ground moves under every island already standing, silently, for tiles nobody has touched. Measured against builds this repo shipped, one 256 window: c04881e differs from today in 1367 of 65536 faces, 239 of them soft ground the island would then refuse to let anybody pack.

title: A bare face shows the rock it is made of
why: Reported: ore and seams that break the surface drew as plain grey rock. A tile dug bare gets the kind written into its data byte, on both sides; a tile the generator lays down as rock does not — the kind goes in the rock array and the byte stays at nought. The drawing read the byte, so a thousand seams a window were invisible while mining and prospecting knew about them all along.

title: The wild mix is the mix the weights ask for
why: Reported as never having seen a mola. The stocker picked a tile, rolled what stood up on it, and threw the roll away when the ground was wrong for it — so a species came out as common as its weight times the share of the island that suits it. A mola wants metal under it, metal is a seventh of the ground, and a mola was one in two hundred.

title: The Wildermon window lists your own wildermon
why: Reported as a new player seeing everybody's wildermon in their Wildermon window before taming anything. The island sends every tame one near you, marked yours or not, and the window listed all that were not wild; the journal's five species, the post list and the herd's best tier counted the same way.

title: A wildermon can come into the world rare
why: Asked for: a wildermon rolls rarity at a made thing's odds, and a rare one is 1.5x the size with 1.2x the stats and better odds of good traits; supreme 2x and 1.4x; fantastic 3x and 1.6x; and the whole beast shimmers like rare gear. Both sides roll it, keep it, multiply every channel of its blood by it the same way, and the browser draws it that much bigger and says what it is worth.

title: A spring fills its hollow and spills down to the next
why: Asked for: player-made ponds, streams and waterfalls above the sea. A spring dug at the bottom of a hollow fills it to the lowest point of its rim and runs downhill into the next hollow, and so on to the sea. Both sides settle the same land into the same ponds and streams, the island keeps them as water to every rule, and the work is done when the land changes, never on the tick.

title: A pool dug in a foundation is water, and a spring in it spills over its edge
why: Asked for: "Allow pools to be dug in foundations". A poured slab takes a pool broken out of it, water to every rule; one dug beside it poured to the same top is the same pool; and a spring dug in one goes over its lowest edge, down the slab to the ground or into a pool below, and on as any spring's water does. Both sides settle the same slabs into the same water.

title: The water drawn into a pond's lip lies only on the pond's water, laid with it
why: Reported: "water can appear clipped over terrain as in my cliff next to the waterfall". A pond going over one corner of a cliff edge, the edge beside it a little below its surface: the water drawn into the lip was carried two tiles along the dry edge both ways. It runs out past each end of the sill as far as the pond's shore does, and on along the lip only over the pond's own water. Reported again with the cliff edge raised above the pond: the same water was laid over the rim and its moss in front of the pond. It is laid with the pond's water, tile by tile and only over it; the lip lays only its mouth.

title: Stones across the water, a fountain that is a well, and lilies that keep the year
why: Asked for: a water garden -- stepping stones, a tiered fountain, water lilies and lotus. Stones go down where the water is no deeper than twice swimming depth, and nobody on them swims: in_deep_water and the browser's body agree, and rpc_move walks them without a pull. A fountain is a well to every rule. A lily or a lotus is planted in still water and roots, flowers, seeds and dies back with the island's year, on both sides alike, pinned to each season in turn; every refusal is said in the same words.

title: A building stands on piers over a slope and over the water, the same on both sides
why: Asked for: a building may take in tiles that slope or lie under shallow water by standing its ground floor on piers, walked at the deck's height on both sides, with the ground under it left alone. One scene -- a sea shelving deep, a pond with a lily in it, a bank and a terrace -- is put to both: every tile planned on or refused, under the same deck; three buildings carried out a tile at a time; the piers' bill in every material; walls, stairs and a deck taken up; walking on, off and along a deck, and a cart and a hull refused one; the ground under it dug, flattened, packed and paved; a crate on it, Examine and the ground read.

title: An aqueduct carries a spring's water over a valley into its basin
why: Asked for: aqueducts -- a stone bridge whose deck is a channel, from a pond or a pool to a basin no higher. Both sides refuse the same plans in the same words, take the whole of the water at its head along it, fill a hollow at its foot at the channel's rate, keep a fountain full and send a full pool's water on over its edge; and dry up the same way when the head falls or the foot goes. Its piers are walls to a pool's water and stand in the way along it, the ground under its arches is the ground, and nothing is planted, planned or dug under a span, on both sides alike.

title: Nobody on the move is pulled back for going as fast as they can
why: Reported as players rubberbanding when they move quickly. The island held a ship to her build's pace while the browser sails her with the wind, her quality and the hands at her helm, so a good ship in a good wind was pulled back every second; and other people were drawn jumping, cut short mid-walk by everybody else's words and pulled back to rows a second old. Told twice a second, somebody walking is drawn moving every frame, never backwards, never more than a word and a half behind; a rune gate is a jump.

title: A rack takes eight crates and says which spots are full
why: Reported as no way to add crates to a crate shelf. The rules knew about racks; the only way to reach the placing was the tile menu, and a click on a tile with furniture on it opens the piece's menu instead — so eight spots nobody could load, holding crates nobody could click.

title: A plan is marked out round its outline
why: Reported as "there's currently nothing at all to show it's a plan". Everything drawn for a building hangs off a wall or a floor, and a fresh plan has neither, so a footprint was ground like any other ground. It is marked out with stakes and string now, and this is the rule that says where: the outline, once per border.

title: The ground is the one on the chart
why: And that the ground both generators agree on is the ground that was drawn. They would agree just as contentedly on relief nobody asked for: `land` and `depth` are multipliers on the chart's own range, and if that range is not what they were written for, the shortfall is quietly made up by the ridged noise.

title: A thing in your hands crosses from the island whole
why: Reported as "players cannot drink from water skins or fill them". Both sides of that were right and the seam between them was not: `play.ts` read six fields off an item row and dropped seven, so a full skin arrived empty. Nothing measured the seam, which is why a bug that broke seven features at once went unseen.

title: What the island's answers say has happened to you
why: Reported as "floating text only shows for climbing". The renderer draws a floater off a skill gain or a hit, both of which come out of the code that does the thing — and on an island the island does it. Climbing is earned off your own feet, which is why it was the one left. The change is worked out from what already arrives.

title: What a rare thing is, and what a pass can turn one into
why: Every rarity number is crossed from `RARITIES` into `rarity_def`, so the two sides agree by construction — right up until somebody writes one out again by hand. `improve_ceiling` did: it said a rare thing could be bettered 4 past your skill while the table, the browser and the island's own examine line all said 5. This puts the two lists side by side, and rolls the ladder a quarter of a million times to show a pass is one step up or none.

title: Every goal the journal counts is a note the island writes
why: Forty-six of the journal's eighty-five goals count things done, and every one of those counts was written by a browser performer — so on an island not one of them could ever tick, and nothing said so. The notes are the island's now, and this is what says when one goes missing: a goal whose key nobody sets looks exactly like a goal nobody has got round to.

title: Where the water starts, and where a pick stops
why: Reported as a copper vein that would not be mined, with "You cannot mine below the water level" and no water drawn on it. The island's half of that is measured in island.sql against the rules; this is the browser's half — that water is drawn from the first unit below the line, so one dug corner is already a puddle, and that the allowance both sides read is one number and not two.

title: The land read is the same island as the history replayed
why: Two roads to one place, which is the thing this island has been bitten by more than any other. A join used to work the island out from its seed and lay every row of `tile_change` over it, which costs the area that has ever been worked and climbs for ever; it reads the land itself now, which costs what the square is. Both are driven here over one island with the same digging done to it and compared byte for byte — heights, soil, tiles, data and rock — and so is the seam that makes the swap safe: the cursor the window is read at is taken before the land, so a spadeful turned in between is replayed as well as read rather than lost between the two.

title: What a ground read is allowed to forget
why: `rpc_ground` answers in two halves and `sawGround` has two kinds of key: ones the answer always carries, which may be cleared and replaced, and ones it carries only on the reconcile, which may not. Getting that wrong does not look like a bug in the reading — it looks like the thing itself flickering, once a second, for ever. It has been got wrong twice in that one function now, for the settlements and then for the crops, so it is a test rather than a comment: `undefined` is "nothing said about this" and an empty list is "nothing is there", and they are not the same answer.

title: What is lying on the ground reaches a browser
why: The ground answer never carried a thing lying on the grass, and the browser's map of the ground was only its own rules' to write, which do not run on an island: a corpse was in Postgres and drawn by nobody. The answer carries `lying` now, and this hands `sawGround` one as the island sends it.

title: Concrete goes on plain rock, never on a seam
why: A corner holds up four tiles, and a vein under any of them raised with concrete would be ore for ever. The browser's door, asked about a shelf of bare rock with a vein, the coal, and plain rock under it.

title: You turn on whatever bites you
why: A bite used to mark you and hurt you and that was all. Bitten in a game of its own, a body swings at the thing with what it had been doing first in line behind it; a second bite changes nothing; a nip from a tame one is no fight.

title: A window that draws the trades, and the answers it is drawn from
why: Five doors existed for a day with nothing drawing them. The trades window draws them now and works out none of it for itself, which makes the shape of the answer a contract: a field renamed on the island is a blank card in the browser, and nothing else in the suite would say so. This asks that every field the panel reads is on every card, that the two sides describe all twenty-four trades identically, and that the three write-doors do what the buttons promise -- take a trade of each, buy a node, and find a rite on the fighting one and none on the craft one.

title: Five stores that take one sort of thing
why: Ore, logs, dirt, shards and wool go in the raw bin; a plank, a brick, a lump, a hatchet and wheat are refused in the island's words. The craft material bin is its opposite number off the same bill, and takes exactly what the other refuses -- so the pair of them partitions the materials: nothing goes in both, every material goes in one, and the split is forty-five raw to a hundred worked on both sides. It is measured in kilograms rather than counted, which the island agrees to the unit: 250,000 nails, 1,250 planks or 416 timbers in the same bin. And the three that came after: a larder of 250 that takes food and drink, and the flour, dough and cornmeal a kitchen bakes from -- those three being `material` still, so the craft bin takes them as well -- and a seed bin and a sprout bin of a hundred kilograms each, which is 5,000 wheat seeds or 1,000 sprouts. All five ask one field, `furniture_def.takes`, and both sides refuse in the same words to the dash.

title: An anvil off the island keeps its metal
why: The island hands an anvil's metal in `sub`, as its own rules read it. A copper anvil set down on an island came to a browser as an iron one; now it is the anvil it was poured as.

title: What the ground says about a cut it will not take
why: A slope refusal carries its numbers on both sides, ground inside somebody else's stake is refused, flattening steps round a corner of bare rock instead of stopping at it, a level taken stops a run of goes on the mark, and a spadeful comes out of the crate.

title: What a go teaches the body, and what it does not
why: Eating, drinking and carrying things about are not work: both sides name the same twenty-five jobs that teach the body nothing, and a loaf eaten in a game of its own leaves every stat where it was.

title: Nothing walks under half again what it can carry
why: Asked for: "when inventory is above 150% cap, movement speed becomes 0". What a body carries was the browser's own business, and a stop only one side holds is a stop the other can decline — so the two numbers behind it are generated into the island and this puts the browser's to them before loading a body until it cannot walk.

title: A field gets sown, and a load goes where there is room for it
why: Reported: "seavic isn't planting seeds that are in crates on deed, and rabba are just overdelivering to the full deed crate instead of bringing anything to the empty crate." Both were the island being thinner than the browser, so both questions go to both sides over the same settlement, the same field and the same seed.

title: The store you aimed at is the store it goes in
why: Reported off a crate rack: "trying to place any items in any of the pine crates gives an error that the maple crate is full". Putting a thing away never said which container, so it went into whichever stood nearest — which on a rack of eight is always the same one.

title: What fits goes in, and the rest stays in your pack
why: Asked for: "when trying to put 48 items in a container that has room for 13, deposit 13 and reject the 35." It was all or nothing, so the way through was to count the difference yourself and split the stack by hand.

title: Which storey, which side, and how many to go
why: Reported: "cant plan roof on when conditions are met. make sure that doors and window walls etc count as elligible walls if completed." They do; what was wrong was a refusal that named neither the storey it meant nor the side that was short.

title: A wall is a box, and the face you see is the one you are standing on
why: Reported: "walls are paper thin and have no character." A wall is a box now rather than a curtain, and which of its two faces is drawn is worked out per wall from the camera — one line that, with the sign backwards, would put every wall on the island half a tile out.

title: An archway, in each material
why: Asked for: "add a new doorway type, Arch, in each material." A type is offered in every material by construction, so what is worth checking is that both sides charge the same for it in all twelve — and that it hangs nothing, which is the whole of what it is.

title: A go that missed still teaches you, and says so
why: Reported: "i'm not getting any smelting experience for failed smelting." The experience was there; nobody was saying so. The line was written by hand at the end of a performer and a failed craft returned before reaching it, so this asks both halves — what a miss is worth against a landing, and that the same sentence comes out of both sides for the same ruined crucible.

title: Head work raises mind logic
why: Mind logic rose from crafts, restoring and books and nothing else, so its knacks came to crafters alone. A go of prospecting, an offering to a wild creature, a scroll set and a hoard dug up raise it now, on both sides, each by its base under the same name.

title: Knacks on the move roll at the share of a go they teach
why: Asked for: less knack gain for driving, swimming and the like, because they are raised a tick at a time -- a second, a tile, a step -- and every tick rolled a whole go's odds. Both sides now roll at the tick's base over a go's, and every other trade as before.

title: The last job asked for, asked for again
why: Asked for: a repeat-last-action key for the tedious jobs, casting nails among them. The browser asks again through the same door every ask goes through, so this holds what it asks for and with what.

title: A foundation is the same slab on both sides
why: Concrete foundations: level ground poured into a slope, leaving the slope alone. Two numbers decide everything about one — what it costs, which is the hole it fills priced by the step, and how deep the deepest part of that pour is, which is what it asks of your masonry — and both are worked out twice, once a side. So the same tiles are put to both and the answers held against each other.

title: Every tool can be made a second time
why: Reported: "there does not seem to be a way to make a chisel / mould for chisel." Four of the ten tools you come ashore with could never be made again by anybody, and every tool wears — so each was a countdown, and the chisel's ran out first because the whole of Stonework wants one. Nothing was wrong in any one file; a tool simply had no row anywhere, which is hard to notice by reading. So it is counted: everything that can put a tool in your hands is walked, and anything left over is a tool nobody can replace.

title: What the bench gives back, and what a click is worth
why: Three reports in one message, all about the moment a go ends. "free body control gains from examining as well as keeping/putting back items" — thirty-two jobs that cost no wind and take no time were paying a body for them. "my bronze anvil isn't letting me improve it saying that i need bronze, but i have 37 bronze lumps on me ... actually it looks like everything i try to improve is telling me that" — the island looked for the metal in a column a lump does not use, so nothing in anybody's pack was ever the right material. "i've made a lot of whetstones and haven't managed anything other than QL 1" — a tool roll that missed paid nothing at all instead of paying what the tool was worth. Each is measured here rather than eyeballed, and the middle one is put to the island too, because that is the side it was reported from.

title: A storey stands on what is under it
why: A building could be ten storeys of logs: nothing anywhere asked what the stuff would stand, so twelve materials differed only in what they cost and what colour they came out. Each says now how many storeys of it hold up, the shortest material in a building caps the whole of it, nothing heavier goes over something lighter, and raising a storey takes ten of the trade below for every one above the first. The cart half is the browser's alone, since the island has never had an opinion about where wheels may go.

title: A room with walls round it and a roof over it
why: A roof cost half a wall, took the same work, and did nothing at all: what you left on the floor of a finished house rotted at the rate it rotted at in a field, and the only thing on the island that ever sheltered anything was a sack. There are rooms now — everywhere you reach without crossing a wall — and a room walled all round with something over it is indoors, worth a tenth of the rot and a third again of a night's sleep. The sweep never charged for a deed either, which the browser always had; both tenths are one function now. And a roof has a shape: gable, hip or a flat deck you can walk out onto.

title: A cellar under the ground floor
why: Nothing went under a building: the ground floor was the bottom of it, and the coolest place to keep food was a room, at a tenth of the rot. A finished building's ground-floor tile is dug out now, the soil with a shovel and the rock under it with a pick, a storey down, giving what digging and mining that ground would, by somebody inside the building; a staircase or a ladder from the ground floor is the way down, climbed from its foot and no other side; nothing walks, reaches or digs from one cellar into the cellar of the building next door; what lies down there rots at a twentieth, and a bed down there rests as one indoors does; the ground over it is left as it was, and the building comes down only once it is filled in. Where it meets the rest of a building: no cellar under a deck on piers, no way down over a glasshouse's field, no lantern post down there, no shop counter tended from down there, and no altar down there glowing on the floor over it.

title: Where the body is, told to the island in order
why: The island takes a change of storey only from the tile it heard of last: down from a flight's head onto its foot, up from the foot onto the head. Both steps are said as they happen, and when a word before them was slow to be answered the two went together, the storey change could land first and be refused, and the two sides had the body on different storeys. Against a keeper stubbed on fetch with rpc_move's pull-back and cellar_move_ok: every word waits for the answer to the one before; a word about walking still waiting gives way to a newer one, so a slow link hears a word a round trip and never a backlog; a word on the stairs that the island pulled short of them, or that went unanswered, is said again before the storey change off them, and a storey change that went unanswered before the next word on its storey; an answer on another storey puts the body where the island has it; a late answer changes nothing; a job waits only for a word at the stairs; and a call that never comes back holds the next up for `MOVE_LOST` and no longer.

title: A jetty out over the street, a railing round the roof, a hall on columns
why: A storey stopped at the edge of the ground floor, a flat roof you could walk out on had nothing round it, and the only thing that held anything up was a wall, so there was no such thing as a porch, a balcony or a market roof. A storey above the ground floors out a tile now on the wall under it, open to the storey as a jetty or shut off behind a door as a balcony; a railing goes round the open edges up there and round a flat roof; and a column on each end of a side closes it as a wall does. Every refusal, every storey closed in or left open, every bill, the shelter under a roof on columns, Examine's words and the edge you stop at are put to both sides. Where it meets the rest of a building: a jetty off a building on piers counts from the deck, a column stands on a built deck no heavier than the lightest one and a deck carries it, a deck holds what stands on it, a deck's edge takes a railing; no glass column and no glass over a jetty under a flat roof; no jetty over an aqueduct's span and no aqueduct under a jetty; a cellar is filled in before its columns are asked about; a shop counter a jetty rests on says the jetty first; and no piece stands in a column's corner.

title: Glass in the window, and a colour on the wall
why: Every window on the island has had glass in it since the first day and the glass was never made, never paid for and never once lit: a window wall cost three quarters of a solid one and nothing besides, so glazing was free and a window was cheaper than the wall it was cut into. And everything here comes out the colour of what it was made of, so a street of twelve materials is a street of twelve colours; paint is the first thing a builder gets to choose.

title: The pile on the site, and a bridge to a storey
why: A builder carried everything — twenty-four logs for six walls, at what a log weighs — while the crate they were tipped into stood on the very tile being worked. And a bridge's ends wanted a bank or a poured slab, both of them ground, so two towers a tile apart were a staircase down, a walk across the yard and a staircase up.

title: A ramp bridge, from one storey up to another
why: Asked: "Is it possible to plan a bridge stretching up from 1st to 3rd floor?" A bridge's ends had to be within END_SLOP of each other and on one storey. Past END_SLOP its deck is a ramp now, at RAMP_SLOPE a tile at most. Both sides allow exactly that slope and refuse one more in the same words, allow the ground to storey 3 over the tiles that climb wants and refuse one fewer, set out the same bridge with the same bill, stand a body at the same height along it, and walk it up and down at the storeys of its ends.

title: A bridge of each wall material, one to three lanes wide
why: Asked for: stone and timber bridges by wall material, their length, bays and drop off the material's storeys and heft, one to three lanes wide. Both sides allow each material's longest deck and deepest drop and refuse one more in the same words, lay the same bays and piers, bill a span a lane and a pier a storey of drop, let a wagon onto two lanes and not one, furniture onto a three-lane deck's outer lanes and not its middle, and turn the old wooden bridge and stone arch into a plank and a stone brick one.

title: Eight ways round, not two
why: Reported: "when changing camera angles models just twist in place." Every animal is drawn in profile and the only thing the view could do with that was mirror it, so a beast heading north and one heading east were the same picture and walking the camera round one showed you the same flank. What the angle decides now is how much of the length you are looking along, with the far end riding up the screen because it is further away. Furniture had the same fault in a different shape: a piece was an iso box and every drawing put its front on the two faces nearest you, so a wardrobe showed its doors from everywhere and had no back. A piece is a model now, put on the screen through the camera's own turn, which is checked against the camera itself. Both failures are silent — a sign backwards and every beast on the island walks backwards — so the eight are counted rather than eyeballed.

title: Each wildermon line's models and voice fetched when wanted, and let go of when not
why: The models were a quarter of the game's code, all loaded before the island was asked for anything. Each line is fetched the first time a body of it is drawn, its voice the first time one is in earshot, and a line not drawn for a while lets go of its pieces and pictures. Checked: every line and voice comes, nothing imports one by name (which would put it back in what every player loads at the start), and a line let go of is made again the same.

title: A settlement full of wildermon and walls draws them once, not every frame
why: Solara stood under ten frames a second at any zoom: its wildermon's standing pictures came to five times what was kept, so each was drawn again just before it was wanted, and an altar in view after dark had the night mixed at four times the pixels. Then "still massive fps drops": every floor drawn afresh after dark, the shade round every wall cut to every tile every frame, and a wheel of the zoom making every crated wildermon and every piece again at every step. Drawn in Chrome on the page's own clock, on Solara as the island counted it: a second loop round must make next to no canvases, the night must be mixed at the lights' share, a settled frame must draw next to no floor or shade afresh, and a wheel of the zoom must stretch what it had rather than make it all again.

title: A mark on a clip fires once as the body's clip time passes it
why: Action effects fire from marks on the clips, worked out on every screen from the body's own clip time with nothing sent. Followed per body: once a run of a loop; a frame drawn again or a clock put right fires nothing twice; a new go fires again; a leap, a change of clip or a body unseen starts afresh with no storm of effects; a timed go fitted to its length fires once a run; the mirrored clip fires from the other hand; the point is on the weapon and the same each time.

title: Action effects with thirty at work, and thirty in a fight, keep to their share of the particles and cost little
why: Sparks off a one-handed blow and chips off a pick fire from marks on the clips, on the spells' particle pool. Drawn in Chrome on the page's own clock with thirty people fighting or mining: both kinds fire; the particles alive stay within the action effects' share of the pool, asked for far more or not; a spell's particles past that share leave the effects none; a frame with them is within a quarter and 3 ms of one with Effects off; Off fires and adds nothing, Fewer adds less, and on the processor's GL only the marks marked key fire. And thirty in a fight (shields, two-handed weapons, bows, every class of armour, blows on all of them in turn): blocks, blows landing, heavy blows and bows fire, within the same share and margin; on the processor's GL the blocks and the blows landing still fire, the heavy blows and the bows not.

title: Animations Off holds every body and creature still and draws them again only when they change
why: Asked for: a performance setting that turns off all animation, for slow machines. Drawn in Chrome on the page's own clock with thirty people at work and in a fight, eight wildermon (three walking), trees, the sea with a swimmer and a lit fire, three rounds of On and Off in turn: Off draws bodies afresh next to never once nothing changes and ten times fewer than On or better, makes no wildermon pictures once their still poses are drawn, and a frame is no slower than On.

title: Low-end graphics draw the wood flat, less motion stops its sway, and every key is a row
why: Settings for the person at the screen, drawn in Chrome on a wood of solid oaks and rose bushes: Low-end graphics, and Low power on a phone, draw every tree and bush flat, Full and Fast draw them solid; Motion Reduced, or System under prefers-reduced-motion, stops the sway on every frame and leaves a 2 s transition at next to nothing; a Text size preset scales the interface by its share; every row of the Keys tab takes a new key and goes back with its reset; no key is under two things out of the box, and a kept table with one is mended; every key main.ts handles is a row.

title: Somebody else is drawn once, in a saddle or at the reins
why: "I appear double to other players, even my chat bubble is doubled": up on Thistlekit and at a wagon's reins at once, drawn on the saddle and on the box. Drawn in Chrome at three zooms and every eighth of a turn: up on a mount, at the reins, and both, the name is written once a frame.

title: The world's hover box comes back
why: "After playing for a bit, mouseovers go away and don't return until refresh": a thing's card in the pack held the tooltip until its row's mouseleave, which a row taken from under the pointer never has; a note pinned by the Tile window's i held it until the i was pressed again. Drawn in Chrome with the real mouse: the ground said, a row's card, the logs taken from the pack under the pointer and the ground said again at two places, and a pinned note put away by a press on the world.

title: The pack, the skill book and the belt drawn once a frame
why: The island's words on the pack come a row at a time, and on the book a skill at a time: drawn once at the next frame, and not at all while the window is shut. Drawn in Chrome: a dozen words draw the Inventory list once; shut, none, and once as it opens; three skills rising show at the next frame, each row flashing; and the pack, the book and the belt show what each shows drawn afresh.

title: The Wildermon window's Care tab
why: Drawn in Chrome over a herd of twelve in every state: the window opens on Care, the needs read worst first, each fix asks the island for the job the creature menu would, Feed hungry feeds one at a time and each once, Assign selected assigns the ticked, and on a phone nothing runs off the side of the window.

title: The island heard from where the camera is standing
why: There was no sound in this game at all — no AudioContext anywhere in the source — so a pickaxe in marble and a needle in linen were both silence. Everything is synthesised now, and placed in the mix off the screen rather than out of the world, so the camera is the ear and what you have looked away from goes quiet. Whether any of it sounds good is what ears are for. What is measured here is that every one of the three hundred and ninety-three jobs that costs time or wind is either given a noise or named as making none — a job missing from the tables would be silent, and silently — and that the mix is the shape it claims: centre loud, either side panned opposite ways, and far enough off the view not started at all.

title: The soundtrack reads, makes and loops
why: A piano soundtrack generated in the browser (src/audio/music). Every bar of every track reads and ends inside its bar, every note is on its instrument's keys, every instrument makes finite notes with no click in and no cut-off out, and a pass is the same each time it is played but different each time round.

title: A walk puts the work down, and a piece can be asked for a quality
why: Walking anywhere used to throw the whole queue away — moveTo cancelled, rpc_cancel emptied act_queue — so a builder with four walls lined up who stepped to the woodpile came back to an empty head. It holds now: the job in hand goes back to the front and nothing restarts itself, because being dragged back across a yard you crossed on purpose is worse than losing the list. And a piece can be asked for a quality instead of a count of passes, which is the wrong unit: what a pass is worth falls away as the piece gets better. That is one refusal on each side, and the two are compared here word for word, because a ceiling the browser honours and the island does not is a button that works until it doesn't.

title: A run is not a fast walk, and a wall knows whose room it is in
why: walkPhase advances quicker when you move quicker, so a horse at a gallop took a body's steps — more of them a second, the same reach, never leaving the ground. Three things separate a run from a walk and all three now come off one number read from the ground a thing actually covers. The load-bearing check is the first: at a walk every one of the fifty-two drawings is what it was, bit for bit. Only a run is new. And the sign of the lean, because getting it backwards would have everything on the island sprinting while leaning away from where it is going — obvious in a picture, invisible in a diff. Plus the cutaway, which used to fade the near walls of the whole building you stood in, the far bedroom's included.

title: Somebody coming ashore is told what to do and what decides it
why: There is no tutorial on this island and never has been. The journal is eighty-five goals all on screen at once, which is a good list and a poor answer to "what now": a list says everything at the same volume. The first chapter is read out one goal at a time now, in as many words as it takes, and stands down for good once the stake is in the ground. And one rule is said out loud that never was: your skill is the ceiling and your tool decides how often you reach it. That was reported as the game being broken — "i've made a lot of whetstones and haven't managed anything other than QL 1" — which is what a rule looks like from outside when nobody has said it.

title: A herd keeps together, and a hunter keeps to its country
why: Nothing kept a wild animal anywhere: a wander target was drawn a tile and a half from wherever it last got to, for ever, so an island's wildlife had no geography at all. Everything wild has a home now, and a herd is not a list anywhere — it is a shared home, taken from the nearest of its own kind at the moment it arrives. And the leash was tied where a chase began, which is right for a hunter you walked in on and wrong for one that had already strayed: that one would take you thirty tiles further still. Both measures are asked now and the first to run out ends it. Put to both sides, because the wild is thought about on whichever of them is doing the thinking, and a herd that holds together in a browser and scatters on an island is worse than no herd at all.

title: What you are on a settlement, and what opens for you
why: `deed_member` was a flat list: in or out, and everybody in it could dig up the gardens, empty the stores and pull the walls down. Four ranks now, and the shaping question goes through `may_shape` rather than "are you on the roll". And everything anybody built was open to everybody. A padlock is forged with no key and cuts one when it is fitted; the number they share is the padlock's own id. The one way back in is the ground — the founder of the settlement a store stands on — because a game where losing a small item costs you a building is a game nobody enjoys. Both refusals are compared word for word across the two sides. And "two people on one job", which I suggested was missing and is not, is measured so it stays true.

title: Coins that buy something, three ways
why: Coins have existed since there was an anvil to strike them on and have never bought anything, because there was nothing to buy them with and nobody to buy from. One number settles the money — a gold coin is worth ten silver — and three ways goods change hands, because they answer three different questions: a deal is two people standing together, a stall is for when you are not there, and a parcel is for when neither of you is. The arithmetic is checked on both sides, including that change comes back in the fewest coins and that a purse which cannot cover a price pays nothing at all rather than part of it. And that the two functions which mint and destroy coins are the island's alone: a door onto either would be a door onto making money.

title: A trade window between two people
why: Two people standing together ask, say yes, put things and silver on their sides and both accept; then everything changes hands in one transaction or nothing does. Every refusal -- a thing gone from the pack, worn, kept back, short of silver, too far apart, gone -- is held to the browser's words and told to both. A change takes both Accepts back, an Accept sent twice or four at once moves nothing twice, and nobody outside a trade can read or touch it.

title: Everybody you may write to, each of them once
why: Friends, the people off your own land, and anybody who has written to you are three questions with the same answers in them, and the Letters tab laid them end to end: a friend you had also invited home was two rows of the same person. The Friends tab, three lines away in the same file, had always folded them through a `Set`. So the rule is a function now rather than a line inside the drawing, and this asks it the question the screenshot asked.

title: What Look says is coming for a tree, the same on both sides
why: "The woods turn over in 9 hours, and it will be shrivelled. Prune it to keep it." is one sentence written twice, once a side. A solo world hears the browser's and an island the island's, and a player who plays both should never be able to tell which — so every stage of the age table is put to both, and the hour-words at their thresholds, where a sentence turns.

title: A furnace off the island reads the way one you built yourself does
why: The island writes a finished piece as {def, ql, count, extra} and a job as {makes, left, total, ql}; the browser's item has an id and its job an item. The list was taken as it came, cast and not looked at, and a right-click on a smelter with a finished lump in it threw out of the click handler and locked the input. So a smelter and a kiln are handed over exactly as the island hands them, and asked what the menu asks.

title: A slope you can stand on is the same slope on both sides
why: The standing cap is written twice — `standsOn` and `standSlope` in the browser, `walk_share` and `creature_tile_ok` on the island — so the same dug ground is put to both: a tile seventy steep and one fifty, a walker at climbing nought and then fifty asking to step off the flat into each, and a wild thing asked whether it would stand there; and the seventy again with a flight of garden steps laid on it, which anybody stands on up to `steps_most`.

title: A flight of garden steps is the same flight on both sides
why: Laid, walked and taken up by the browser's rules in a solo world and by the island's on an island, so the same ground is put to both: a dozen shapes of tile and whether each takes a flight, the doors of laying one in stone and in timber a missing thing at a time, a flight laid and taken up with every roll passing, walking onto one at sixty-four, eighty and past it, a cart on the reins, a wild thing standing on it, the climbing a step teaches, and the names.

title: A flag flies its colour and an arch its roses, the same on both sides
why: A piece set down on an island dropped its dye, so a banner dyed in the pack stood undyed and a sail went up white. So a dyed flagpole and banner are set down and picked up on both sides and read back off the ground read; and a rose arch's roses grow from when it was set down, which the island hands over for an arch and nothing else, which a night's sleep does not move, and which setting it down again starts over.

title: The crafting window offers a choice of wood
why: Asked for: a pack with oak and pine in it, and a row that lets you say which the piece is to be made of. `materialChoices` lists the woods carried for the recipe, `recipeStatus` takes the one the row is set to, the clicked stack still wins over it, and the thing made comes out of the wood the row said.

title: A craft reaches into the stores around you
why: Asked for: "When crafting, allow the ingredients to be used from any container within 3 tiles." A pack, a satchel and a spread of stores round the body, put to both sides: what is at hand, the order it is spent in, a run that carries on past the stack it started on and stops when its wood runs out (not on in another), the wood the window says, and nothing out of reach, locked, thrown away, for sale, put by or somebody else's.

title: Eight more trees that bear, held to their islands
why: The species of a tree is the low nibble and the top bit of its tile byte now, and every byte from before has to read as it did; the chart's regions each grow their own kinds and never another's; an island of your own grows them all.

title: Thirty-four traits for a fight, each in four grades
why: Fighting blood is a name and a grade rolled for it: thirty-four names in all four tiers, a share of the wild's rolls, never two grades of one name on an animal, and a line that climbs a grade of its own name.

title: Twelve more traits on the channels there were, hearth-bred healing the herd
why: Traits part A: eleven plain traits and thorned, a fighting name in four grades. Each at its rarity with its figures and card the same on both sides, each rolled in the wild at its rarity on both, and hearth-bred's communal healing the same in the island's settle and the browser's.

title: Traits part B, stamina, rest, breeding, care and food, on both sides
why: Eight traits on eight new channels: each card the same words on both sides, each rolled at its tier, and each channel changing its rule by the same number: goes before a worker tires, its rest, a dam's time, a second young, a mutation, a slot drawn from the pair, care lost and what a meal counts for.

title: Night-eyed, deep-pocketed, lucky finder and settler, the same on both sides
why: Four traits on four new channels: what the night takes of a kept one's sight, a load more a trip, a seek go's relic find chance and an idle worker's wait, communal. Each card, each rolled at its tier, and each rule caused on the island and read in the browser.

title: Six traits for a fight, on six channels of their own
why: Venom-proof, quick-clotting, fearless, crushing, ripping and quick-recovering: on the table at their tiers, their cards the same on both sides, rolled in the wild, and each channel changing its rule by the same number on both sides: venom taken, what a bleed takes, a Fear's running, an ability's rest, and the chances a blow lands heavy or bleeds, counted over a few hundred blows.

title: A quarter of the cycle dark, on both sides
why: "On the full day cycle, it shouldn't be half night half day, it should be 3/4 day and 1/4 night." It was forty-two per cent dark, which reads as half. Dawn moves to three and dusk to nine, so eighteen hours sit between them with noon exactly in the middle. The second half of this is why it was possible to get wrong: the island's `darkness` held 7, 19, 21 and 5 written out by hand, the same bug `hour_of_day` had when it held 1440. It reads the generated `dawn_hour()` and `dusk_hour()` now, and the whole day is asked of both sides in three-minute steps.

title: Seed in the crate, and one you keep put down in one action
why: "Seavics also move seeds to storage if not using them when working deed": the seed from a harvest went into the browser's `pouch`, which is not a thing a person can open, and into the furrow on the island, where it lay under the next crop for ever. It is a load like any other now on both sides, and this follows it to the crate. And "add a cull option on tamed wildermon to kill them with one action", which until now meant swinging at your own livestock until it stopped. Same carcass, one action, and a refusal for anything wild or anything across the island.

title: A shore face is work and the sea floor is not
why: "Allow mola to mine ore, seams and rock at up to -10 water level just like players." Three rules were in the way and only one of them was about depth. The browser asked whether a body could stand on the tile, which allows one unit of water; this island asked nothing at all, so a worker here would set about the sea floor at forty fathoms; and both sides had `rock_height > 1`, which reads as "is there rock here" and is really the waterline again, so no depth allowance anywhere else could have helped. The person's rule now, on both: ten units of water, the same floor under the pick, a bank on any of the eight sides to swing from, and a face too deep to stand on worked from that bank.

title: Who pays for the wildlife
why: "Something is severely delaying server responses." It was this: a block of country is stocked the first time anybody walks into it, and that used to happen inside `rpc_move` — the call a walking browser makes constantly — so the walker stood still for a second and a half. PostgREST answers eight at a time, so three people crossing fresh country held three of those eight and everything else queued behind them. It is on `stock_tick` now, a clock of its own with a lock of its own, putting out the block underfoot and the eight around it so the country is ready before anybody arrives. The assertion that matters here is the exact one: walk thirty steps across a block never stocked and nothing may appear. That is what fails if stocking is ever put back on a request path. The density is pinned here too, because a constant changed in TypeScript once made the server five times slower with every test still green.

title: The stocking clock, cheaper and the same
why: `stock_tick` asks once whether any block round anybody is owed and stops there when none is; `near_tile` reads each line it looks at once. On an island of its own: `near_tile` gives the answer it gave before at every point sampled, and ninety minutes of the clock as it was and as it is put out the same blocks on the same turns, the same wildlife in the same places, with the same stamps.

title: A spadeful you could not put down
why: "Allow dropping dirt on the ground as a pile." Dirt was the one thing in the game a person could pick up and then not put back down: both sides refused it by name, on the reasoning that dirt belongs in a hole. It does, and it also belongs in a heap beside the hole while you decide which hole.

title: A function the planner could not see into
why: Postgres folds a `language sql` scalar function into its caller and refuses when the body holds a sublink. `max_health` held one, so every creature in every `rpc_creatures` answer paid a whole function call with the entire row handed in as a composite — and handed in again to `beast_mul` underneath. This pins both the property that makes them fold and the numbers they answer.

title: The woods turn over once, at dawn, and finish
why: `tree-tick` was wound at ten-minute intervals against a job with one day's work in it, and the one go a day with work to do was being killed by the statement timeout. The reason is a cliff that opens on the fourth line of an island: a four-kilobyte line is stored packed, `select into` copies it packed, and once plpgsql keeps the plan every `get_byte` unpacks the whole line again to read one byte. Measured here rather than asserted, because it is one character away from coming back. And the morning the woods die, which that fix never met: a quarter of the wood going at once was ten minutes of reading bytes where they lie -- the corners, the ground round every stump, every line a sapling went into. So the corners are asked for unpacked, the seeds for a band read once, `b_i16` for an expression the planner inlines with the same answer for all 65,536 values, a die-off on a real island for stumps, saplings and a record that matches, and the tick for one island a go.

title: A day in the woods in parts, the same day
why: A go of `tree_tick` was a whole island's day in one transaction, 98 seconds at worst on the live island, holding every line it had written. It is parts of a second now, each committed, carried on from `private.tree_run`. On an island of its own: the day as it was, the day in the smallest parts there are and the day in one go leave the same ground byte for byte and the same record, from one seed; a spot built on between picking and planting takes no sapling; and the tick carries on a day under way first.

title: The island's year is the same year on both sides
why: Four seasons of seven days, turning with the woods. The browser works the season out for itself and so does the island; asked about the same moments, every six hours for a year and a second either side of each turn, they must say the same season and day.

title: Feet wear the same trails on both sides
why: Grass, lawn, steppe, tundra and moss wear where people walk: a step on your own feet is a point of wear, and at the threshold the tile is a trail keeping what it was; each turn of the woods takes wear off and gives a trail with none left back. The same rows are walked through rpc_move and through the browser's own body: the same tiles wear by the same amounts and turn at the same step, a bridge, a building, a foundation, a storey and a saddle wear nothing, the most is kept without a write, the woods' turn does the same on both sides and is told, and a step costs one keyed write.

title: A trail is drawn under water
why: "trails do not appear to draw over tiles with water": the island wears trails into ground a pond or the sea covers, and the renderer left the path out on every wet tile. Drawn in Chrome, a trail through a pond and one down a beach into the sea, each tile worn against the same tile as grass: the path on a tile the pond's edge crosses and under its shallows, less of it under its deepest middle, up to the sea's edge and on the first tile under it.

title: Wildflowers bloom in the same places on both sides
why: Where grass flowers and how thick is worked out from where it is, by the page that draws it and by the island that lets it be picked: the same drift to the last whole number on every tile of four seeds, the same clumps in every season, counted in the same year. Pick flowers gives the same wildflowers and the same words on both sides, and the first turn of a new year makes a picked tile flower again on both, and tells everybody.

title: Stone greens on the same clock on both sides, and clears the same
why: Asked for off a picture of a grey castle: ivy up the walls and moss on the paving, the statues, the slabs and the stone bridges, bare the day they are built and as green as they get a fortnight on. The island keeps when each began and carries it with the thing; the browser works the days out and draws them. This puts the same moments to both clocks, a day's edge to the quarter second either side, checks what starts one on each side, feeds a real ground read to a browser and holds every thing's days to the island's, and asks Clear the ivy and Scrub the moss of three people on and off a settlement: the same refusals, the same words when done, and the same bare stone after.

title: Crops grow through the year, and planters grow them indoors, the same on both sides
why: Asked for: "outdoor seasonal growths for crops, with planters that can be grown indoors regardless of season at a much slower rate." A field grows at its season's share of a crop's pace and not at all in winter; a planter at one share in every season. Both sides count a field's growth on a field clock worked out from the moment alone, and are held to each other bit for bit at thousands of moments round the turns; crops straddling the turns and whole winters settle to the same stage and stage start; a wait is said in the same words; and a planter is sown, tended, harvested and pulled up through the doors on both sides.

title: Fruit, bushes and forage keep their seasons, the same on both sides
why: Every fruit tree, every bush a sickle cuts and the seasonal wild forage has its seasons in one table (`src/game/fruiting.ts`), which the island reads off the definitions. This holds the island's table and every sentence to the browser's; counts the season the same way at moments round the turns and before the first spring, when everything bears; and in each of the four seasons, held on the island and stood still in the browser, picks four trees and cuts two bushes on both sides -- the same refusal out of season, the same fruit and words in it, the same Examine -- rolls the forage tables on both and finds only what is in season, and asks whether a plucka would climb the tree.

title: Sand, clay, peat and tar workers collect, the same on both sides
why: A Mudlet on clay at water level with no soil left: it would work it, a go gives clay and leaves the ground as it was, and the tile is not worked again straight after -- on both sides.

title: A well's water reaches the browser as it stands
why: A well drawn dry a hundred seconds ago is sent with what it has drawn since, and one drawn dry a day ago is sent full (`rpc_ground`).

title: A glasshouse grows its crops the year round, the same on both sides
why: A roof laid in glass, on a pitched roof and nowhere else; a building of one storey under nothing but finished glass is a glasshouse, whose ground is tilled and sown like a field, and what grows there grows at the whole of its pace in every season, winter included, on a glass clock of its own. Both sides are held to each other on that clock bit for bit, on crops settled across every turn of the year and held in each season, and on a stage start carried onto the glass clock and back to the microsecond without losing a second of what it had grown; and a glasshouse is built, tilled, sown, tended, unroofed and roofed again, brought on by Bounty, slept through and harvested through the doors on both sides, refused in the same words; Examine says what it is; a building with a field in it takes no roof but glass and no storey until the field is cleared; a wall down, or a fence in its place, unmakes a glasshouse; and a poured slab under one is not tilled.

title: A solid wall is laid in glass, and nothing else of glass but a roof
why: Glass is a solid wall and a pitched roof and nothing else. A solid wall of it is planned on both sides at a solid wall's bill; every other wall type, fence, floor kind and a column refused in glass in the same words; a hod carrier holding glass is sent to it; and a one-storey building walled all round in glass, each wall built a unit a go through the doors, under a glass roof, is a glasshouse on both sides, and not while its last wall is going up.

title: A garden bed is a field on any storey, open to the sky or under glass
why: A floor of garden bed, laid as a floor and nothing else, at its bill through `floorBill` and with iron ribbons only; finished, sown, tended and harvested on the ground and on storey 2 from the storey stood on, on the glass clock in a winter, open to the sky or under glass; covered by a floor or a roof not of glass, refused a sowing, its crop held on the still clock and grown on from there when uncovered; one crop a tile; taken up with its bed; worked by a farm worker up the stairs; a glasshouse field and a planter as they were.

title: A wall changed where it stands
why: Change wall: another type or material planned on a wall of a building, offered and allowed on the wall storey 3 rests on, which Remove refuses. The wall standing stays finished, shut and carrying while the change is built a unit a go, and is the new wall with the last of it; a type that carries nothing is refused in Remove's words, a material too light for the walls above as a Repoint is, and the rest as Plan wall refuses them, all in the same words on both sides. A wall still going up is planned again in place.

title: A team stays in the traces until it is taken out
why: "hitching wildermon to the wagon doesn't seem to be working". On an island the hitch was written and nothing read it: the settle every second walked a companion back to its keeper and sent a worker to its trade, its belly went on emptying, the bell called it off the shafts, and the browser was never told it was hitched, who was driving or who had a cart by the shafts. This asks both sides that one in the traces stays there, is nobody's quarry and gets no hungrier until it is taken out; that everything that would send it elsewhere says why not; and that a vehicle is anybody's to use.

title: The wagon beside the furnace
why: "pouring a mould, as an action that requires ingredients, should be pulling the iron from the adjacent wagon as it is within 3 tiles". A craft reached into the stores around you and no station did: a smelter, a kiln, a fire, an oven, an anvil, a barrel and bettering a thing all asked for what was in your hands. They take what they use up from the same stock a craft does now, on both sides, and a cart, a wagon or a boat counts as a store whoever built it. This sets one spread round a body and asks every station of it, and that the stores it may not touch are not touched.

title: What a craft may take is the player's to say
why: "add a toggle in settings for allowing or disallowing crafting from nearby containers. add another setting that disallows the automatic use of any rare material in crafting." The browser keeps both in Settings and tells the island (`rpc_craft_prefs`), which keeps them on the body because it is the island that spends a job's stock. This asks both sides: with the stores out nothing in them is at hand, even named; with rare stock spared the craft and the fire pass a rare stack over but take it when pointed at it; and with the rare not spared it is used like any other.

title: What you gather goes in the cart
why: "When doing actions from the cart, all gathered materials should go right to the cart." With the reins of a cart or wagon, or a small cart by the shafts, what a gathering job brings up goes into it as far as it has room, and the rest into the pack, with the cart said to be full once an ask. This digs from a wagon on both sides, fills one to two short, empties a creel into it, pulls a small cart, and asks that a boat and bare feet still gather into the pack.

title: Let go over a container
why: "Allow drag and drop from the player inventory directly to a container by dragging the item to the asset model and releasing." A pack row let go over a crate or a store in the world asks the door the store window's drop uses, naming the store. This asks that a crate in reach takes the stack at once, that one across the yard is walked to and takes it (not the one beside you, which is where a name out of reach used to fall back to), that a chest does too, and that on an island the island is asked on arrival.

title: Seeing into a house, and out of one
why: "i can see through the doors, but only one tile deep", and not to the night's radius either. The line of sight took every tile a building stood on for a solid block. Walls stand on borders, so a line is now followed border by border and only a finished solid wall stops it. This builds one house with a door, a window, an arch and a half wall and asks, by day and by night, that you see in through them and out of them as far as you see in the open, the whole of the inside from its middle, and that a solid wall still hides what is behind it.

title: The last spadeful, and one fault one job
why: "something just broke, no actions are working". `take_spoil` and `site_take` set the last one of a stack to a count of 0, which the item table refuses, so a cart's last spadeful raised an error -- and `world_tick` settles everybody in one transaction, so that one job failed every round for everyone. This takes the last one out of a crate, a cart and a site's pile, settles the reported job through the clock, and puts a fault in one body's way and then in a sweep, asking that the round finishes, that everybody else's work settles, and that the faulty job stops, says why, and is kept where the deploy reports it.

title: A citizen of somebody else's settlement may found their own
why: "i disbanded my settlement so i could make a new one but it's still telling me i can't because i already have a deed ... i think it must be because i'm a citizen of oceanport". The island refuses a stake only to a founder; the browser refused anybody it held a settlement for, and with none of your own that is one you were asked onto. This asks both sides that a settlement of your own still refuses a second in the same words, that a mayor, builder or guest of another is offered the stake, that the border is the one refusal left, and that a builder founds their own on the island and stays a builder of the other. And the other way round: "I don't have an invite option for you and [another player] since we're already in a deed". The Social window offered Invite only to strangers; this asks that somebody on another roll is offered and asked, and that "already asked", a full roll and Move in with no room are refused in the same words by the browser, reading the island's own `rpc_social`, and by `rpc_invite`.

title: A settlement previewed before founding, and the Runestones' rings on the map
why: "Before the stake is spent, the player can see where the settlement would be and whether it would be refused." On Bigness, with somebody else's settlement put down for it: a token one short of the spacing from it, one fifty tiles from the Crownstone and one that is neither. The browser's preview, handed the island's own rpc_settlements answer, says what act_refusal says for each, word for word, as founding there does. And the map lists every stone runestone_centres has, by name at its centre, its ring deed_stone_gap() out from its edge.

title: Mayors invite, and ranks are set
why: `deed_member.role` held mayor, builder or guest and nothing ever wrote it, so nobody could be made a mayor, and inviting and sending away were the founder's alone. This asks that the founder makes a mayor, a builder and a guest; that a mayor ranks builders and guests and cannot make, unmake or send away a mayor or touch the founder; that nobody changes their own rank; that a mayor invites and a builder does not; that the one asked sees who asked and both the mayor and the founder hear the answer; and that the old two-argument `rpc_invite` still asks onto the caller's own. Every refusal is compared word for word with the browser's rule reading the island's own `rpc_social`.

title: The Skills window's sliders, off the rules
why: Asked for: a slider in the Skills window for everything a skill changes, every skill, each track from the skill's own starting value (20 for a characteristic) to the top. Every skill has sliders, every value reads, none is flat, reading them leaves the skill where it was, and carry weight, time per go, success chance and a sword's blow are the rules' own.

title: Ask to join a settlement at its token
why: Asked for: "Allow players to request to join a settlement at the totem." A stranger standing on a settlement asks at its token; its founder and every rank holding Invite hear it and answer it in the Social window; the one who asked may take it back. This asks every refusal on both ends, who hears it and who may answer, the rank a newcomer is let in at, and that taking up an invitation clears the ask. The browser's "Stand on X to ask." and full-roll refusal are compared word for word with the island's.

title: A work post takes a wildermon as Hitch does, in the same words on both sides
why: "Bug: workposts aren't working. Make it work almost like a Hitch, able to select the wildermon following or held in crates in inventory in a menu on the post." One following you and one in a crate in the pack are each set to a post and work out of it; the crated one comes out at the post. Four refusals are compared word for word with the browser's.

title: Logged on and off, said to everybody, in the words the browser reads
why: "Add a banner like when entering a deed when a player logs on or off. Add a text line in Talk when a player logs on or off." Washing ashore, coming back and logging out idle each say it once, to the whole island; a step says nothing; the browser reads who and which.

title: Accounts - addresses noted, new bodies per connection, keeper doors want the code
why: The join and the beat note the caller's address (once per 10 min when known), the clock forgets one unseen 90 days; one connection makes 3 new bodies in 24 h and is refused the 4th, a keeper never; with a verified second factor every keeper door but am_i refuses aal1 in the browser's words and opens to aal2.

title: Six more relics put to use, the same on both sides
why: "Old collar, old bridle, seed jar, old whetstone, makers stamp, rune tablet." Each restores into a thing of its own; the collar and bridle fitted once on a wildermon, the whetstone honing, the jar opening to seeds, the tablet read into a skill, the stamp pressed for its goes; refusals and lines word for word.

title: A bronze mirror copies a parent's best trait to its young, the same on both sides
why: "Copy a trait to a newborn: at breeding, the newborn gets the parent's best trait at that parent's value instead of rolling it. Used up on the birth." The mark, its refusals, the best trait and its tie, the draw with copies, the covering and the birth.

title: An ancient brace, a post worker's meal and scarcer seed, the same on both sides
why: "Ancient Brace ... action speed by 1% per, up to 50 uses", "wildermon on a workpost will feed themselves ... from containers in work range", "30% chance of getting 1 [seed] per harvest".

title: Wildermon gear, a pack, a harness and barding, the same on both sides
why: "wildermon gear (#17)": fitted and removed from its menu, its size only; a pack's load a trip, a harness's team pace and barding's damage taken, scaled by QL; worn a use, repaired once taken off.

title: Body stamina grows the stamina bar, the same on both sides
why: "Body stamina should also increase the bar. 2x at 100". The bar is 1 at the starting mark and 2 at a hundred; a dig and a second of rest move the same share of it in the browser as on the island.

title: Awareness, more uses, more sources and a start at 20, the same on both sides
why: "1 add those [uses], 2 add those [sources], 3 start at 20, 4 keep [the curve], 5 add both". Notice range, track reach, hit chance in the dark and the husbandry a trait needs at 20, 60 and 100; a tile walked, a forage and a track teach the same on both sides.

title: Soul strength, its uses and its sources, the same on both sides
why: "1. Add to those other uses. 2. Add those sources as well. 3. Keep small. 4. Fix text." At soul strength 20, 60 and 100: the same tame chance, favour per prayer, Calm per sitting and Beastmaster heal, blow and bonus on both sides; a prayer, a sitting and a sacrifice each teach soul strength an offering's gain.

title: Ranks of your own, the founder's to make, in the same words on both sides
why: "Allow the founder to establish ranks and advanced permissions for all citizen ranks." Every settlement has its own ranks now, up to the cap besides its founder, each named, ordered and given any of the powers in `RANK_POWERS`, with Mayor, Builder and Guest to start with doing exactly what they did. This asks that the island's list of powers, cap, name limit and "you may" words are the browser's; that every settlement, a new one too, starts with the three and newcomers join as Builder; that only the founder makes, renames, moves and deletes ranks, with each refusal; that taking a power away really stops its action and giving it really allows it -- digging, a crate, a lock, inviting, sending away, setting a rank, renaming and upgrading -- and that disbanding stays the founder's; that a rank acts only on those below it; that every refusal is the browser's word for word over the island's own `rpc_social`; and that only a settlement's citizens read its ranks.

title: A settlement at a glance, its visitor log and its orders, on the island and in the window
why: "Put ranks, permissions, upkeep and specialties in one clear panel, plus a visitor log and guard settings." On an island of its own: Visitor log and Wildermon orders are the browser's powers and the log's limits its own; a stranger walking onto a settlement is written down once an hour, never its founder or a citizen, and a visit past the keeping goes at the sweep; the watch lists each visitor once to the founder and a rank with Visitor log and says the browser's sentence to anybody else; the orders set every settlement worker, a citizen's too, for a rank allowed them, and a wildermon assigned after takes them; writing a visit costs rpc_move little (timed). Then, in Chrome, the Settlement window drawn from the island's own answers: six tabs, every rank's permissions on one grid a click each, upkeep soonest first, each trade against a specialty with Assign, the orders, the visitors, and on a phone nothing off the side of the window.

title: A settlement's notices, posted by a rank that may and read by its citizens alone
why: "Citizens holding a rank power can post short notices to their settlement, and every citizen sees new ones when they come ashore." This asks that the limits and every sentence are the browser's; that a Mayor posts, a Builder does not until the founder ticks Post notices and not again once it is unticked; that a stranger can neither post, take down nor read, and is handed nothing coming ashore; that an empty notice and one past the longest are refused and runs of spaces become one; that the board keeps the newest and drops the oldest; that a citizen ashore hears a new notice in the log and one away is shown every unseen one coming ashore, once; that one away longer than NOTICE_MAIL_DAYS is sent each as a letter from whoever posted it, as it goes up or by the hourly sweep, once, and is not shown it again coming ashore; and that no browser reads the tables.

title: Work a settlement wants, delivered at its token, and its ledger
why: "The founder, or a rank with Set work, lists work wanted; citizens deliver toward it, credited in a settlement ledger." This asks that only a rank holding Set work sets and takes down work, with every refusal of a work the browser's word for word; that a stranger can neither set, deliver nor read; that delivering takes the lowest quality at the work's least or better, splits a stack for the last few, and refuses too far, too poor, a full deed crate and none; that the rows are moved into the deed crate and not copied, and nothing worn, kept back or holding something goes; that each delivery is credited to whoever made it and a work with all it wants is closed and written in the ledger; and that no browser reads the tables.

title: Shared settlement stores
why: A crate or a piece of storage furniture on a settlement, marked one of its stores by its founder or a rank holding Keep the stores, opens for the founder and the ranks holding Use the stores, padlock or not, and for nobody else, key or not. This asks that the log's cap and which pieces may be a store are the same on both sides; that marking and unmarking are refused to a rank without the power, a stranger, a store on no settlement, a stall, and twice, and allowed to the rank and the founder; that a rank with Use the stores takes from and puts into a padlocked crate and chest without the key, on the island and in the browser; that a rank without it and a stranger holding the key are refused in the same words on both sides, and a take-all that lands after is refused too; that every take and put is logged -- who, what, how many, which way -- read by the founder and Keep the stores only, and never longer than the cap; that only whoever set a store down and the founder pick it up or turn it; that a craft never draws on one; and that disbanding unmarks them.

title: Leaving a settlement you were asked onto
why: "add a leave settlement option so citizens can quit oceanport". The island has had `rpc_leave_deed`; the settlement's own menu gave a citizen the founder's entries and no way off the roll. The menu and the Settlement window now offer Leave, found by the token's place through the social answer. This asks that the social answer gives the founder and the token and `rollAt` finds it (not your own, not a tile that is not a token), that a citizen is told the upgrade is the founder's, that leaving asks first in words that name the settlement and who is told, and that on the island the builder leaves by that founder, is off the roll, is told, the founder is told, and there is nothing left there to leave.

title: Butchering is learnt by butchering, and decides what comes off
why: "Add the Butchering skill that gains experience from the matching option. Butchering skill determines ql of Butchering output". On an island a go at Butcher never raised the skill -- the butcher branch had no `skill_raise` -- and what came off was scaled down again by the corpse's own quality. With a knife of QL 100, whose roll always lands, this asks both sides that a go raises the skill, that everything comes off at the skill whatever the carcass's QL, that the log line says the QL, and that the menu's Butcher line gives the range for the knife in hand, from the same rule.

title: Every tool wears with its action
why: "Butchering knife should take dmg from butchering", then "sweep other tools for missing actions". The browser wears every action's tool; on the island the butcher, shear, till, investigate, repoint, ivy, moss and the foundation's four wore nothing. Asked of every action with a tool, off the island's own performers.

title: A wildermon nobody has named is called what it is
why: Reported: old names after the visual overhauls, and stages not named for what they evolved into once tamed. One that goes only by one of its kind's own names is called its kind at its stage on any change to it; one its keeper named keeps the name.

title: A harder tame teaches more taming
why: Asked for: "Taming attempts on harder to tame wildermon should grant more experience". An offering, a trap's catch taken out and the Call of the Wild teach their gain times 1 + taming needed / tame_hard(), the same for every kind at every stage on both sides.

title: Life stages on the seasons' scale, and death of old age
why: Asked for: "Scale life stages to match the 90-day seasons. 90d days at old and the wildermon dies of old age." young_for, old_at and old_for the same on both sides; one past its old age dies, leaves its carcass and its keeper is told; one still in it lives.

title: A stored wildermon crate says who is in it
why: Asked for: "Add wildermon names to wildermon crates when in all storage spots like stalls". A piece's things, a crate's things and a counter's goods carry the crate's wildermon and its name, and the browser names the crate by it.

title: A wildermon's light goes where it goes, and not into a crate
why: Reported as a glimmoth's glow following a player a poll behind after crating it, and left on a hillside once the crate was stored in a stall. The night's lights gave every creature in the list its light, one shut in a crate too. Lit only while out in the world.

title: A wildermon past the first goes into a creature crate, and out of it again
why: Asked for: "Wildermon can be tamed to be set to active if currently no active wildermon, but any additional wildermon cannot be tamed unless the player carries a creature crate ... Wildermon can no longer be Kept at Token. Interacting with a creature crate allows you to pick it up / place it, assign the creature to active, or assign the creature to work the deed."
