why: Sewing (needle), fitting (hammer), cutting and harvesting (sickle), tending and clearing (rake), paving and mixing (trowel), glazing and painting (brush): each job's tool on the browser's recipe or action and the island's, and each refused without it in the same words on both sides; workers still need none.

title: Every job with a tool wears it
why: Every job with a tool in the browser has it on the island with the same `wear`; a go of each wears its best copy once in the browser; every go on the island is private.act_go's, and a go of one job of each family wears by the browser's amount, once; improving wears each tool; a worker's errand wears nothing.

title: A pack beast's panniers are a store
why: The Packlet line's panniers by stage (200, 500, 1000, and a hauling trait) on both sides; put in, full and taken out as a chest's are; counted by a craft and by building within reach and not past it; whose they are, by the keeper's settlement and its ranks; and crated, released, culled or swapped into a crate only once empty, in the same words on both sides. On the island, turned loose they are set down and dead they go with it.

title: The Smith's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Smith's eighteen measured on the island with the dice taken out where they can be: the smelter's glass, mix, melt, mould and pour; the anvil's hammer, second heat, nails and tool heads; the marks it beats into a blade, a hauberk and a breastplate and what each does, carried into a sword whoever fits it; ingots poured and counted as their lumps; the stores a forge reaches, a pass of Improve, the queue and a quench; and the browser reading the same.

title: Melt down all, and what comes back said
why: All of a stack too big for one furnaceful: what fits goes in, the rest stays in the pack and the line says how many did not fit; several things melted, and what came out told to whoever melted it in one line, not to the maker; drawn off; the same words in the browser, off the shared phrasing.

title: The Forester's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Forester's eighteen measured on the island with the dice taken out where they can be: Cut down's time, strokes, stroke that lands, and what a felled tree gives and leaves; a bush's shafts; the sprouts, the planting, the graft and one more fruit; the three new jobs with every refusal, Tap Resin's day included; Look counting the strokes; and the browser's pace through brush and its menus.

title: The Farmer's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Farmer's eighteen measured on the island with the dice taken out where they can be: the seed kept, the pace a crop is sown at and grown at, the field's last crop; the harvest's bumper, two more, rarity, grass and store; the quern's flour and fruit, the milk, the load and the rake; the three patch jobs with every refusal; a worker's harvest; and the browser's menus and numbers.

title: The Cook's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Cook's eighteen measured on the island with the dice taken out where they can be: the pot's quality, one more and ingredient back; the four marks on a dish, what they fill, feed, give and rot, and the pile they make; the fuller table; food set down cool; the knife's share, cuts and bait; a strong brew stamped, drawn off, drunk, poured together and emptied; the pantry's reach; broth and spirit with their refusals; a taste; and the browser's words and numbers beside the island's.

title: The Tailor's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Tailor's eighteen measured on the island, the dice put either side of a perk's number where it is a chance: the shears' wool; the spindle's time and third length and the loom's two yarn; a failed check held up, spared or lost; a rare cap; the lye left in the bucket; the marks on bags, tack, yokes, nets and creels and what each then does; the lighter pack; the workshop's reach; a patch with its refusals; the tent, built and slept in; and the browser's words and numbers beside the island's.

title: The Herdsman's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Herdsman's eighteen measured on the island, the dice put either side of a perk's number where it is a chance: a wild one's odds, its coaxing and any food offered; a brushing's care and healing; the keeper's numbers stamped on what they keep and read by its hunger, its care, its work and its age; a pairing's rest, its carrying, twins, the sex asked for and the blood drawn; the lighter crate; the Stud Book's odds; and the browser's words and numbers beside the island's.

title: The Naturalist's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Naturalist's eighteen measured on the island, the dice put either side of a perk's number where it is a chance: a look over the ground, its passes, its empty ground and its rare finds; a cut of grass and of reeds; the pot's time, pots, dyestuff, failures, ink and covers; a dressing's time, its slips, its quick hands, and one put on somebody else; the three remedies made and used; a hive filling; and the browser's words and numbers beside the island's.

title: The Fisher's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Fisher's eighteen measured on the island, the dice put either side of a perk's number where it is a chance: a line's and a net's reach; a fish staying on, the bait kept, the bait's pull and food on the hook; the big fish, the rare ones and the fuller net; the time and the wear; a deeper creel, fish cooled where they lie, smoked fish, the journal's line on the water and a pond stocking itself; and the browser's words and numbers beside the island's.

title: The Mender's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Mender's eighteen measured on the island, the dice put either side of a perk's number where it is a chance: a go of Repair and the time off the floor under it; the wear on a tool, armour, a shield and a sword; a post and a snare standing longer for their setter; restoring surer, gentler, finer, rarer, a better roll and a better tier; the floor under improving; the kit and the sealant; and the browser's words and numbers beside the island's.

title: The Artisan's perks, each where its rule is
why: Each of the Artisan's eighteen measured on the island, the dice put either side of a perk's number where it is a chance: a stone set surer and kept whole; a pot's serving and a jar's keeping, carried through the kiln; a ring and a circlet worn; the rock's odds and its six more stones; a focus's wear and force; a book's teaching and wear, and a trade book; the amphora and what is in a bag set down; the potter's wheel; the glaze; and the browser's words and numbers beside the island's.

title: A portcullis, a drawbridge and a hidden door, the same on both sides
why: Asked for: a portcullis raised and lowered that stops everything but the eye when it is down; a drawbridge worked from its winch that cannot be crossed when it is up; and a door that is a solid wall to everybody its lock does not admit -- "the island must never tell a browser it is a door unless that player is admitted". This asks what each costs, what the ground read says to four people (the founder, a key holder, a builder with no key and a stranger) and that the wall table cannot be read round it, what a browser fed that read lets through and sees through at every state of both gates, who may raise and lower each in the same words on both sides, the island's own walk over the drawbridge, who may pull a bridge down on a settlement and off one, and that planning a hidden door leaves nothing on the player row anybody may read, writes the one line a solid wall's plan writes and moves no counter further than it -- each ask waiting on its own border, lapsing, and never kept for a plan that is refused -- and all of it beside what the other batches build: decks on piers, aqueducts, cellars, jetties, columns, railings and glasshouses.

title: A fence stands on a shore where its border is above the water
why: Reported: Plan fence on a path's border with a waterway, 0.1 m up, refused "Not in water." because a tile beside it had water on it. Only a corner of the border under the sea or a pond refuses it now, and 'No room for posts.' asks the dry side: the reported border, a corner at and under the sea, a border out in it, a pond's border above, at and under its level, a tree on either side and a border on land, the same on both sides; the reported fence planned and built on both, and finished, it stops a step across it either way.

title: A rune gate is laid, passed and lit the same on both sides
why: Two rune pillars under a lintel on a border of their own, in stone brick and nothing else with a light mote in each pillar, that shut nothing out; their runes light while a citizen of the settlement they stand on is in the opening. This asks what it is and costs on both sides, every material against every wall type in the same words, planning one on both sides, what goes through it, the rolls the island sends whoever is ashore (founder, mayors and builders of each settlement a rune gate stands on, never a guest), and a browser fed them lighting it for a citizen in reach and not for a guest or a stranger, fading out when they go.

title: A memorial stone, engraved with somebody's own words, the same on both sides
why: Built with masonry and a trowel and set down like any piece. A stone chisel cuts a line of up to 72 characters into it, cleaned as talk is, by whoever set it down or anybody of the settlement it stands on, never by somebody a keeper has muted; every refusal in the same words; a new line over the old; Examine reads it back in quotes; and the line goes with the stone, picked up into the pack, said on Examine there, set down again, through the ground read, the pack's row and a save.

title: Vineyards and wine that ages, the same on both sides
why: A cutting off a thorn bush with a sickle, planted on a trellis on soil and refused off it; the vine too young, then picked in autumn for the grapes its picker's forestry gives and refused in every other season with when it fruits, at the same held moments in the same words; grape wine brewed from its grapes, its ageing stamped as it is set going; and the QL a barrel of it is at after so many days in a cellar and out, to the last bit on both sides, capped, said on Examine and drunk at.

title: A bucket keeps its brew's QL, and mead ages, the same on both sides
why: Each brew's rate and cap the same on both sides; a bucket drawn off grape wine kept thirteen days at the barrel's aged QL, off the top of a pile; one off ale at the ale's QL and one off water at its own; the aged bucket poured back into an empty barrel at its QL, not ageing there, and one poured into a barrel of the same at the average by litres; milk at two QLs poured in and drawn back out at the average by litres, as every liquid but water keeps its QL on both sides; mead set going stamped, and its QL so many days in a cellar and out to the last bit, capped, said on Examine.

title: A brewer's spring brews in ×0.75 the time, the same on both sides
why: Each brew's time in a barrel and in a brewer's spring the same on both sides; Set a water mote refused without a mote, while a brew works, a second time, out of reach, on a well and on nothing, in the same words; set, one mote used up, said on Examine; ale in it done at ×0.75 the time and not a second before, where the plain barrel's still works; mead's ageing stamped at its end; the island sending the mark and the seconds left.

title: Maps drawn, studied and copied, the same on both sides
why: Draw a map on a sheet of papyrus: the square round the tile you stand on, as far each way as its QL reaches, written on the map. Study it and the square is on the reader's map (`charted`, and a `charted` line the browser puts on its fog); Copy it and the copy is no better than the map or the sheet. Every refusal in the same words, and Examine says what it holds.

title: Milk, butter and cheese, the same on both sides
why: A butter churn built with carpentry and set down; a bucket of milk churned at it into the pats of butter the browser says, the bucket back; a pastry baked with butter and cheese pressed, their counts; butter and cheese keeping longer than milk by their decay, every row the same on both sides. And every kind that is milked filling a bucket a milking, at the quality and in the words of the browser.

title: Whey from cheese, fed to a creature, the same on both sides
why: Cheese pressed hands the bucket back full of whey, and a failure hands it back empty. A bucket of whey is fed to a kept creature of any kind for the share of its hunger the browser names, the bucket back empty at its quality; its own diet still fills a meal, Feed takes the thing it is asked to, and the refusal is in the same words.

title: A skep, filling with honey and beeswax off the wildflowers in reach, the same on both sides
why: Woven by ropemaking with a carving knife and set down like any piece. What it has made is worked out from the moment it was set down or emptied: a honey every so many hours for each clump of wildflowers in reach, each season at its own flowers, nothing in winter, nothing with none in reach, up to what it holds. Take honey and Examine, their words and refusals, on both sides.

title: A masterwork signed by its maker, once, the same on both sides
why: One thing made at the signing QL or better carries its maker's name, and one made under it does not: a mallet carved at the bench on both sides, and rare work as ever. Sign refused under the QL, for rare work under it, for a pile and a piece of furniture, for anybody but its maker, for blank words and for somebody a keeper has muted, in the same words; the line cleaned as talk is and cut at the longest; signed once and refused after; and Examine saying the maker and the line on both sides, through the row and a save.

title: Dyed glass, and a window the colour of its panes, the same on both sides
why: A glass panel takes a dye at its own litres; one of a pile is dyed and the rest stay clear, in the same words. A window glazed with red panels is red and a bay with blue ones blue on the wall row on both sides, one glazed clear stays clear, and the ground read brings each window's colour to every browser that sees it.

title: A tame woola is sheared from its menu, the same on both sides
why: Shear was never on a creature's menu, and the island never sent a keeper how much fleece had grown back. This asks that it sends it, to the keeper only; that the browser takes it off the row; that no knife and too little fleece are refused in the same words on both sides; and that a full fleece gives its wool and starts again.

title: Your favour is the island's, on coming ashore and on every beat
why: The island kept favour and never sent it, so a reload showed the browser's own nought. This asks that coming ashore hands it over, that every beat says it with its trickle, capped, and that the browser reads both.

title: What is on your table is the island's, through a refresh
why: The page read nutrition off the beat only, and the first beat goes a minute after the join, so a refresh showed all four at nought. This asks that what was eaten is on the row, the join and the first beat, that the browser reads the join's row, and the beat wholesale.

title: A corner the island moves is said to the browsers watching
why: A slab breaking away while mining, a chipped corner and dirt dropped at your feet moved a corner and told nobody until a refresh. This asks that each announces the four tiles that share the corner.

title: A team is not your companion, and is put together out of its crates
why: Reported: once a mon is hitched it still counts as following you, so the next cannot come out of its crate. This asks, on both sides and in the same words, that one in the traces is not your companion, that one in a crate goes straight into a yoke, and that a team comes out with one following you and the rest into empty crates in the pack.

title: A name as you write it
why: Asked: names were all lowercase, because the name was read back out of the sign-in address. This asks that the capitals written are the name shown, that only a casing of the account's own name is kept, that an account may change its capitals and nothing else, and that the browser keeps them as typed and signs in with them folded.

title: Dirt dropped on a kelp bed makes a dirt floor
why: Asked: dropping dirt on a kelp tile should make it dirt. Kelp was not on the list of ground a spadeful buries. This asks, on both sides, that dirt at your feet and on a corner each turn kelp to dirt.

title: Change tile lays what was dropped
why: Reported: clay or sand dropped on dirt left dirt. Both sides: clay, sand and dirt lay their own tile, at a corner and at your feet.

title: Every vessel holds litres, and a liquid is used by the litre
why: Asked for: a bucket of 5 L of water down a litre a dough, lye by the litre, L for what a vessel holds. Both sides: litres out of a bucket, a barrel making up the rest, names and weights by the litre, a full bucket for lye, tanning, a drink, a pour.

title: Every liquid but lye and dye is drunk, out of a barrel, a well, a bucket or a skin
why: Both sides: a bucket of water and of whey drunk out of the pack, a litre and its thirst; lye not offered; a barrel of whey drunk from, of lye or dye "Not drinkable."; the island's list the browser's.

title: I'm stuck on the ground walks a body out of a pocket no walk leaves
why: A tile raised flat above its neighbours: stuck, unstuck to the nearest tile a walk gets out from, walks on; refused mounted and on open ground; up a storey the ground floor as before.

title: A worker fills its keeper's storage and nobody else's
why: Both sides: a worker whose settlement's square reaches over a neighbour's bin fills its own; off a post and where it unloads, never the neighbour's; the neighbour's own worker still does.

title: A sack, a satchel and a backpack are improvable
why: Both sides: of cloth by Tailoring and leather by Leatherworking, the island's list the browser's, every bag a pack on it; a backpack improved; a sack without cloth refused in the same words.

title: Improve and repair, one window
why: Held equipment, Repair all and Hone all the most damaged first; a run of Improve held to one kind of stock uses that kind and no other and stops "Out of iron lump."; a run of cycles uses its count of stock exactly, repaired between whenever a failed pass leaves it over 10. Several pieces in turn, one job each in the queue: a piece over 10 asked as its Repair carrying the run (cycles), which goes in front when the Repair ends; a fourth job refused by a queue of three. Both sides, in the same words and numbers.

title: One device at a time on an account
why: The first seat holds it, a second is refused "Playing on another device.", no seat is not asked, Play here takes over, a stale seat is free; the browser's calls carry the tab's seat.

title: Winter fur, and critter caches found by Tracking
why: Both sides: the fur multiplier, the loot table, draws and picks the same; more fur in winter only; caches laid in winter only, once; a search reads the nearest, names its tile near it; a dig gives its draws and takes it; a second dig and one after winter refused in the same words. The season pinned on each side.

title: A rare thing put into a crate stays rare, a pile of its own
why: Both sides: supreme planks into a crate of plain ones are a supreme pile; plain ones, and a worker's, go onto the plain pile.

title: A mould is the smith's, formed and poured by blacksmithing
why: Asked: pouring moulds should give blacksmithing experience, and a mould's QL when formed should be the smith's and not the sand's. A pour on the island taught nothing at all. This asks that every mould is formed by blacksmithing, that QL 1 sand fired by a good smith makes a good mould, and that a pour and an anvil cast teach it.

title: A vesp tends the hives, as its trade
why: Asked: vesp should work beehives as their trade. A vesp had none, so it could not be set to work a deed. This asks that it can, that it goes to a hive and works there bringing nothing home while the hive fills, and that with no hive in reach it says so.

title: Things of one kind keep one place in a list
why: Three nail moulds came out in whatever order the pack was last rearranged in, and every pour rearranged it. Every tie is broken down to the thing itself, so a list is in one order however the pack under it was shuffled.

title: Flattening wears the shovel, and every job on the ground its tool
why: Reported: flattening with two shovels damaged neither. On an island flattening wore no shovel at all, and four more jobs on the ground wore nothing either. This asks that a go at flattening wears the best shovel by a dig's wear on both sides, so two share it, and that every job on the ground with a tool wears it on the island.

title: Hostile creatures are marked over the trees
why: Asked: threats are hard to see in a mess of trees. Every wild creature of a kind that hunts on sight, and anything hunting you, is drawn in red over what is in front of it with a marker over its head; nothing else is, and none of yours. No database.

title: A wound you point at, and the Health window
why: Asked: a Health window where a wound is clicked to be bandaged or treated, clear about what has to be carried. A dressing, the lye and a salve each picked their own wound; an ask may now name one (Target.wound), and that one is treated or the ask refused saying why, in the same words on both sides. And the window's reckoning: what it offers each wound, what it says is carried and how to make what is not, from the recipes.

title: Building draws on the stores within reach
why: Asked: "building a wall or other building actions should also be able to draw materials from wagon or nearby storage within 3 tiles". A wall and a bridge's span are built out of somebody else's wagon two tiles off, refused with stores turned off and with the wagon four tiles off, the same on both sides.

title: A wall or a floor is built a number of goes at a time
why: Asked: "Allow bulk actions when building structures like walls and floors, e.g. build 5 10 25 50". A log wall's row offers its counts; five goes fit five logs, and fifty finish it and stop, on both sides.

title: The Equipment window's numbers are the fight's own
why: Asked: an Equipment window to drag things on and off a figure of you, with every combat number and the skills behind them. Each number it shows is held against the rule that decides it in a fight, each skill's line against the rule at its start and its next level, and putting on and taking off goes through the pack's jobs. No database.

title: The journal counts only your own work
why: Reported: goals ticked off by another player's work, and some that never tick at all. On an island only the island's counts reach the journal and the traps in view are not rolled here; each goal that read the world in view reads a count of its own, noted on the island for whoever did the thing; and every goal has a how-to. And the first wildermon chapter: a tame and Work around me started on the island meet their goals from the tally the beat carries.

title: Goals done show as done
why: Reported: goals done never show, not after a refresh either. The island's record comes on the first beat, after the journal has opened by itself at What's new; it now redraws the Goals page, a tab turned to Goals is drawn as it stands, a refused beat keeps its ticks, and the island keeps every tick and hands it back.

title: Goals of the wildermon and of a settlement count on the island
why: Thirty-eight goals: bred, evolved, geared and worked wildermon, the Field guide, and what a settlement is built into. Each count is noted on the island for whoever did the thing, and each goal reads it; every goal id is unique and every line filled in.

title: What a browser hands the island is checked and bounded
why: The ten doors that take jsonb refuse a value of the wrong shape in one line naming the door, the argument and the key, and take every shape the browser sends. The set-down jobs are held to their reach, no job reaches past a ceiling, a read reaches 64 tiles round you, and a spawn, an island's name and a price are bounded.

title: An action taken once, however many times it is sent
why: Every call to a door carries a key, the same one when it is tried again after a network error; the island takes a key once, so an order put up twice or a dig asked twice with one key is done once.

title: A stack split without built SQL does what it did
why: barter_split and rpc_work_deliver copy the row itself now; the old SQL is put back beside each and both run on the same things.

title: No SQL is built at run time
why: Every function in public is read, and every EXECUTE in it must run a literal or format() of one with %I and %L only: no ||, no %s, no SQL out of a variable.

title: Thirty-six goals in the crafts, the land and the water
why: Each count a new goal reads is noted on the island for whoever does the thing, where it is done (a walk's through journal_move), and for nobody else; each goal is met by its count or by a state of your own and not before; every goal id in the journal is once.

title: The island's goals, fighting and faith, people and trade
why: Each of the journal's goals for the island, for fighting and faith and for people and trade: the thing done on the island counts for whoever did it, the browser's goal is met on that count and not before, every goal id is unique, and no goal types out a number.

title: Ten conveniences hold to what they say
why: Put away into the stores within reach that hold the like of it, rot times on the ground, eating by yourself, the shopping list's netting, map pins kept, long walks in legs, and a dam's due time told to her keeper only.

title: Ten more hands on a settlement
why: A kemma brushes the herd, a sheela milks and shears it, a salva dresses its hurts, a carra butchers and a tanna tans what is in the stores, a grista mills, a wicka keeps the lanterns, and a brambo, a grazza and a siffa pick bushes, cut grass and pan sand: each the same on both sides, and each saying what it does in numbers.

title: Twelve more hands on a settlement
why: A Snailglow and a potta empty and charge the smelters and the kilns, a cindra rakes ashes and leaches lye, a hoppa brews, a simma cooks, a relka restores, a bedda keeps the planters, and a wurla, a sprigga, an ambra, a petta and a scurra work worms, sprouts, tar, flowers and moss off their tiles: each the same on both sides.

title: Eight more hands on a settlement
why: A rippa saws planks, a chissa chisels stone brick, a mudda shapes clay brick and a flecha fletches arrows at the stores, a papra presses papyrus at a paper press, a glossa glazes the pottery and a dippa fills the empty buckets: each the same on both sides.

title: A spinner, a nail smith and a ribbon smith, and no worker needs a tool
why: An ulva spins yarn at a spindle, a dowse smiths nails and a siffa metal ribbons at an anvil; every crafting worker works with no tool in the stores and wears none that is there: each the same on both sides.

title: A glimmip makes glass lumps at a lit smelter
why: The Glimmip line melts sand from the stores into glass lumps at a lit smelter of yours in reach, charged or not, and not at an unlit one or one out of reach; idle with no sand or no smelter, and says why; learns glassblowing; its third stage makes a lump more a batch: each the same on both sides.

title: Twelve kinds take up new settlement tasks; the ten old guards are gone
why: A dulla cuts moss, a brambo plants vines (the rootle's, gone), a spitta water lilies and lotus, a crakka mixes concrete, a glossa mortar, a carra saws timbers, an awla carves shafts, a scorcha mixes alloys at a lit smelter, a leecha makes bandages, covers and salves, a frosta presses cheese and a whirla churns butter (the forga, cordra and brittla are gone): each the player's own recipe or action, out of the stores and back in; no worker glazes or butchers; the ten former guards have no ability and do not guard; the testa, skulka, gasha, hamma, bashka, executa, shova, howla, marka and wardo are gone, an owned one turned into the kind it became with all else kept (the migration run twice), a wild one gone: each the same on both sides.

title: What a worker makes in place, on its work log
why: A dowse's nails, an ulva's yarn, a rippa's planks and a simma's cooking counted as handled on the day's log; a load carried back counted once: each the same on both sides.

title: A stoker burns tar first, never overfills, and from its second stage works the smelters
why: A stoker fetches tar, then peat, then coal, then any other fuel, from whichever store holds it; only whole pieces that fit, the rest back to the stores; ovens and braziers too; and a Slugember empties your smelters and charges them with ore when no hearth wants fuel: each the same on both sides.

title: Seven that fight
why: A testa draws what is after you onto itself, a skulka strikes harder at what is fighting something else, a gasha bleeds, a thumpa stuns, a spitta leaves venom, an awla goes through a hide, and a sparra may be sparred with: each the same on both sides.

title: A Sparra on a settlement spars with your guards
why: A Sparra set to a settlement picks a guard of yours there, the one that sparred longest ago first, and the guard walks to it and spars: a go at its task, a blow each way, neither below where it yields, the guard learning its level skill and the Sparra its fighting. Yielded ones stand until they have their breath back, a guard drops it for anything wild, and two take turns: the same on both sides, and the words.

title: Abilities on a cooldown
why: Seventeen wildermon each use a fighting trade's spell, or a frost breath, instead of a blow, then rest for the spell's rest: the same numbers on both sides, and never a wild one.

title: The Whispet, out only from 15 October to 15 November
why: A wild one is put down only after dark and only in its season, by the calendar in UTC, and the spawner takes the wild ones off once it is over; one you keep stays. Tamed, it frightens what it fights instead of a blow, and rests: the same on both sides.

title: The Crumbud, out only from 1 December to 25 December
why: A wild one is put down only in its season, by the calendar in UTC, any year, and the spawner takes the wild ones off once it is over; one you keep stays, and the Whispet's season is as it was. Tamed, fighting, it taunts: what is after anybody within its reach, and every hunter and monster there, turns on it, and it rests. The same on both sides, and never a wild one.

title: A skill for every wildermon, and its level is that skill
why: A kind with no trade and no traces learns one of its own by what it does -- sheared, plucked or milked, sparred with, out with you, out after dark -- and every wildermon's level is its skill.

title: Wildermon evolve at 25 and 50
why: A kind that evolves is its second stage from the first level and its third from the second, each multiplying its health, blow, pace and task over the last; the Snufflet, which was the Rabba, first. The same on both sides.

title: Evolved wildermon in the wild, rarely
why: One put out in the wild of a kind that evolves comes in at its second stage one time in WILD_STAGE_ODDS[0] and its third one time in WILD_STAGE_ODDS[1], at a level in that stage's span, named and as big as it; taming it asks WILD_STAGE_TAME more a stage at WILD_STAGE_CHANCE the chance. The same on both sides.

title: Food quality matters
why: A meal of quality q puts FED_LEARN × q/100 on a tame one's learning for FED_FOR, twice for its favourite, the larger of two and never both, and FED_CARE × q/100 on its care; grazing nothing. The same on both sides.

title: Every trade takes about as long to evolve
why: Asked for: "Even out the time to evolve across trades". Each trade's gains at its level skill are multiplied by LEARN_PACE, which this recomputes from a model of each trade's go on the island and holds to what it was derived as; with it every trade's minutes to level 25 and on to 50 are within 35% of the median trade's, unless held at a quarter or four. The island's learn_pace_def is the same table, and a gain at the same roll is the same on both sides. --table prints the minutes.

title: Each stage lets a deed worker do more at once
why: Asked for: "Each stage unlocks something, not just bigger numbers". STAGE_LOADS (1, 2, 3) the same on both sides, and the same trades carrying and handling; a water carrier at its second stage pours twice the litres a trip, a mender mends its stage's number of the most damaged, a brick-maker makes two batches, and a reed cutter walks on to a second load before it goes home -- each go teaching what one go does.

title: A skill of each line's own at its third stage, and a trait slot more at each stage
why: Asked for: "every evolving line gains one perk of its own at its third stage", and "reaching stage 2 opens one more trait slot, and stage 3 one more". STAGE_PERKS the same table on both sides and nothing of it below the third stage; a reed cutter, a water carrier, a Stoneskin's rest, a stun, a shearing and a blow at it; the words; slots 3, 4 and 5, a trait drawn at each evolution, in the wild at a later stage, and the once-over of the island.

title: Deed workers tire, rest, and sleep in a bed of their size
why: TIRE_GOES goes and no more, REST_FOR where it stands, BED_REST of it in a free bed of its class on the settlement (its stage, or its kind's health band for one that does not evolve), and the bed let go when it gets up, is called to heel, crated or killed, or the bed is moved. Every kind's class the same on both sides, and the words.

title: A settlement's worker keeps to its own settlement, beds and all
why: Asked: "wildermon beds will attract wildermon from across the map ... walk across oceans to go sleep and then they cant return", and "wildermon are still leaving settlement to go work on other settlements or steal their materials". A bed only for a worker of its settlement on its ground; a worker's work, pick-ups, stores and planting on its keeper's home settlement (or on none), not one its keeper is a citizen of or a stranger's; and the stranded put back.

title: A worker a day without a meal works at half its pace
why: Its seconds at work since it last ate, counted only while it works and put back by any meal; at UPKEEP_FOR (the island day) a go takes it 1/UNFED_PACE times as long. Both sides, and its card.

title: Three of a trade on a settlement make it a specialty
why: Deed workers of a trade on a settlement, a citizen's among them; at SPECIALTY_AT a go's work time is divided by 1 + SPECIALTY_BONUS. The count measured on an island with a crowd on it, and the words.

title: The browser's errands and the island's reed cutter agree
why: A mender, a water carrier, a hod carrier, a planter, a stoker and a prospector in the browser take a go's work time, and wait after a fetch as the island does; a stoker, a fetcher and a clearer of rot learn the same a go on both sides; and the island's reed cutter cuts 1 and 1 more for every REED_LEVELS, as the browser does.

title: Skills go on past a hundred, for the boards
why: A go is worth what it was up to SKILL_TOP and is divided by PAST_TOP for every point past it; a skill raised at the top goes on past it, everything that uses it reads it no higher than the top, and the boards read the whole of it. The same on both sides.

title: Skill gain ×2 below 10, the multiplied part up to 10
why: EARLY_SKILL_BELOW and EARLY_SKILL_MUL: a go below the mark is doubled, one carried past it doubled ends at it, one at or above it is the curve alone; the island and the browser give the same gain at each, and the watch counts goes at that rate.

title: The island's watch keeps its ledger and raises its flags
why: Every thing made or unmade is counted per day, item and door; the night holds the count against the ledger and flags a forged duplicate or a leak; a sweep flags things passed between accounts on one IP, a body with no break for 20 hours and a skill risen 3 times past what an hour can teach; only a keeper reads them. And what the ledger's triggers add to a craft, a forage and a step.

title: Every door paced, and a walk held to its pace
why: A per-player rate limit on every rpc_* door, by class, with budgets three times what the browser itself sends; a class's burst and then one line, nothing done. And rpc_move over time as well as a word at a time: 1.3 and 1.6 times the pace in tenth-of-a-second steps end at the pace and the slack, a walk at its pace is never pulled, lag, a late word and a hole included, and stone slabs at their own pace. And a word carries the turns of its path (p_via), walked leg by leg: the browser's own walk through a wood, a word every 1, 3 and 5 s, is never held short, where the straight line was held at a tree and put back; the turns are held to the pace along them, and more than walk_via_max of them is refused.

title: The game's clock against the wall's, and a walk's turns
why: A frame's whole wall time walked in tenths (clockSteps), up to two seconds; the island's go on the action bar runs off the wall clock, four seconds on after one frame of four seconds; a walk goes at its pace and no faster, at sixty frames a second and at a frame every 0.3 s (a step's end is no longer let off); a path's steps kept and its turns only the corners. No database.

title: The exact benefit, and where its number comes from
why: Text the player reads says what changes and by how much, and where the rule has the number the text takes it from the rule (CLAUDE.md). This holds texts against the fields they restate, reads every fixed piece of player text in the source for a number written out, and renders the help. It reads the source with the TypeScript compiler, which stays out of the bundle. No database.

title: A Wildermon tab, and a line there for each worker's finished work
why: The log has a Wildermon tab keeping kind wildermon; a tame, a crate shut and opened, a load put away, an evolution and a birth each tell the keeper as wildermon on the island, a refusal stays an error; a load put away says what was stored in the browser's words (work_done_line, workDoneLine); and the functions about wildermon alone say nothing by plain tell.

title: The same thing, asked for at once
why: Two to six identical calls at the same row, each on a connection of its own, let go together from an advisory-lock gate and each held open a moment after its work: take from a crate, put into one, empty one, load a rack, both Accepts of a trade, a stall's buy, a pick-up, a drop, a delivery to settlement work, workers fetching out of the stores, and the pairs of doors that touch one stack at once. Every thing and coin is counted before and after: none made, none lost, no count below one. Seven connections at most, inside the service's default of a hundred.

title: Put all in, in one ask
why: Reported: "Did I crash the server trying to transfer all of my relics to the cart at once?" 150 things put in a crate and in a cart as the browser now asks them (`rpc_act_many`, 30 to an ask), with the clock going: none made or lost, the kept pile kept, rarity and origins as they were, the rest said as did not fit, one line an ask, and the clock never standing waiting on a lock. A round with a body's row held leaves it to the next round (`busy`); a guard's and a hunter's look round for wild things the same as every one read the old way; an instant ask asks its refusal once; and the browser's asks, a few dozen at a time, one after another (`Island.actMany`).

title: The doors, as the security advisors read them
why: Every table in public has row level security; every SECURITY DEFINER function a fixed search_path; anon and authenticated hold nothing on a table but SELECT and execute nothing but rpc_* (anon only rpc_name_free); lock_doors run again takes no exclusive lock. Two islands: nobody reads a row of one they are not on, from any table with a world_id, and a deal only its two sides. rpc_name_free answers 20 a minute per client IP.

title: Permissions, held to a list somebody has read
why: As anon and as authenticated: every table and view in public is in supabase/test/permissions.allow.ts and read on exactly its terms there (nothing, every row, its policy word for word, or through a security_invoker view); neither may insert, update, delete or truncate any of them; neither reads a row but the rulebook's from an island it is not on; the functions each may execute are exactly the list's, and every other one, called, is refused; every SECURITY DEFINER function fixes its search_path; nothing on a sequence or a table in private. A new table or rpc_* fails here until it is written down.

title: Player text, cleaned the same on both sides
why: private.clean_text and src/game/playertext.ts on a list of nasty strings (an RTL override, zero-width characters, a homoglyph Keeper, a 500-character name, a newline injection, <script>): cleaned, cut, folded and judged the same; the refusal in the same words. Through the doors: talk, letters, notices, crate, wildermon, settlement, rank, body, island and account names cleaned, and a name that reads as a keeper or staff refused.

title: Every job says how it ended, and the log hears it
why: Reported: "Sometimes an action completes or fails with no description in the event log." Every action in action_def with its go come round, against a tile, an empty pack, a tile out of reach, a thing held, a thing, a wildermon and a piece gone, and a person: every go tells whoever did it what it did or why it was not done. A run stopped, no wind, a go that says nothing, the queue, stop, walking off, a refusal, a raise, a hushed plan over an area and the mark at the join. And the browser: a line said the first time its number comes, in any order, the beat asking from a floor that waits for late lines, and an ask the island raised on said in the log. And every go asked again before it is done: the shovel gone, no wind, walked out of reach, the thing gone; a perk's reach as asked; a storey job kept to the storey it was asked on, on both sides.

title: A water mote for a spring, a pool, a fish pond, a well and a fountain
why: Asked for: digging a spring takes 1 water mote, and the fountain, pool, pond and well take 1 as well. Dig a spring and Dig a pool refused without one in the same words on both sides, allowed with one, and the mote used up when dug; the fish pond, the well and the tiered fountain have one in their bills, refused without it as a craft is, built with it, and the mote used up. The water mote says what it is spent on.

title: The creatures read sends only what changed, and the same answer for less
why: Asked for: "streamline cpu". The read with its short cuts says what it says with them taken out, key for key; a browser that says neither cursor nor ids gets the list it always got; handed back its cursor and the ids it holds, it is sent exactly what was written since, what it lacks and which went, and a browser laying those holds what the whole answer says after every turn of the clock. Packed, every row unpacks to the whole answer's, key for key.

title: The ground read sends only what changed, and the same answer for less
why: Asked for: "streamline cpu". The read with the water asked only of a well says what it says asking every piece, key for key; a browser that says no cursor gets what it always got; handed back its cursor it is sent what was written since, what came into range or reach, and what moves without a write, and a browser laying those holds what the whole answer says, key for key, after every change. Asked with the creatures in one round trip, each says what it says alone.

title: Everybody ashore is read once a call, and is the list it was
why: The map's list of everybody on the island (folk_ashore, on the ground's slow half) counted everybody online again for every row, so one ask grew with the square of the people on. Held to the old definition row for row: crowded (no places), five online (places), alone (empty); named by accounts; in under half the old time.

title: A page opened before the migrations asks the new way once the island has them
why: Seen live: every creatures read in the old form for half an hour after its migration. The browser's own Island against a stand-in: told the new forms are missing, it asks the old way, and the new way again RETRY_NEWER seconds on, cursor and all, in one round trip.

title: An ancient helm and an ancient short sword, and nothing improves or repairs them
why: Asked for: "ancient Helms and ancient short swords cant be improved or repaired, even with ancient whetstones. Ancient Helms provide +3 tile sight radius. Ancient swords swing 25% faster." The two relics restore into them on both sides; Improve, Repair, a repair kit, Mend and an ancient whetstone refuse either in the same words, none offered in the browser, the thing as it was after; a worker mending the stores passes them by; a plain helm and short sword as ever. Sight +ANCIENT_HELM_SIGHT worn, nothing carried; the swing at ANCIENT_SWORD_SWING a short sword's on both sides; each says so.

title: A statuette enchanted into a patron's statue, and a prayer said with one from the pack
why: Asked for: "The restored statue can be Enchanted using one of each mote to be statue of x diety and can be used for mobile prayer instead of needing to be at an altar". Each patron's statue made with STATUE_MOTES of every element, one of each spent, QL kept; a mote short refused naming what is short, nothing spent; a fragment and no patron refused. A follower prays with it from the pack: prayerWorth at the statue's QL, an altar's of that QL, the wait started and the second prayer refused in the altar's words; another patron's follower, and nobody's, refused; the altar as ever. Both sides in the same words.

title: Wildermon by name on the island, and accounts under the old suffix moved
why: 20261111235900 over the earlier shapes, planted in a transaction it rolls back: an account under the old .invalid suffix at @catgenova.github.io in auth.users and auth.identities, the same uid and the same name; settings, headers, a view, a default, a check, a policy, a trigger, comments, a role setting and rows renamed, case kept; nothing left holding the word; a second run renames nothing; an account named with the word stops it.
